lines.text: Ancient terracotta, bronze-casting kingdoms, colonial rule, civil war and a culture now heard worldwide. This is the story of Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation.
Thousands of years ago, in central Nigeria, the Nok people worked iron and shaped striking terracotta heads, among the oldest sculptures in West Africa.
By the ninth century, craftsmen at Igbo-Ukwu were casting bronzes of astonishing detail, the oldest known in West Africa.
In the south, the Benin Empire grew around its oba in Benin City, famous for the brass works of its guild artists.
To the west, the Yoruba Oyo Empire rose on the strength of its cavalry and its trade, controlling much of the region.
On an island in a lagoon by the Atlantic, a Yoruba settlement grew that would one day be Lagos, Nigeria's great commercial city.
For centuries, Benin's artists made thousands of plaques and heads for the royal court. Their fate, after 1897, is still debated today.
In 1804, the scholar Usman dan Fodio led a holy war against the Hausa kings and founded the Sokoto Caliphate, which ruled much of the north.
Nnamdi Azikiwe, born in 1904, a journalist known as Zik, would lead the independence movement and become Nigeria's first president.
Obafemi Awolowo would lead the Western Region and bring in free primary education, a towering figure of Nigerian politics.
And Ahmadu Bello would become premier of the north and the most powerful politician of the first republic.
In 1914, Britain joined its northern and southern protectorates into one colony, drawing the borders of modern Nigeria.
Chinua Achebe would write Things Fall Apart, about an Igbo community as colonisers arrive, one of the most widely read African novels.
Wole Soyinka, playwright and poet, would become the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, and a fierce critic of dictatorship.
Yakubu Gowon, an army officer, would lead the federal side through the civil war, promising no victor and no vanquished.
Olusegun Obasanjo would hand power to civilians as a military ruler, then return as an elected president two decades later.
Fela Kuti would mix highlife, jazz and funk into Afrobeat, using long songs to defy the generals despite arrests and beatings.
Bola Tinubu, born in 1952, would govern Lagos State and later be elected president of Nigeria.
Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, an economist, would rise to lead the World Trade Organization.
In 1956, oil was struck in the Niger Delta. Within twenty years it paid for most of the state, bringing wealth and spills alike.
On the first of October 1960, Nigeria became independent from Britain, a nation of hundreds of peoples.
But after coups in 1966, the south-east broke away in 1967 as the Republic of Biafra.
Civil war followed. Blockade and famine killed perhaps a million people before Biafra surrendered in 1970.
Jay-Jay Okocha, born in 1973, would dazzle crowds with his tricks for the Super Eagles in three World Cups.
In 1976, Nigeria chose to build a new capital in the middle of the country, Abuja, which took over from Lagos in 1991.
That same year Nwankwo Kanu was born. He would lead Nigeria to Olympic football gold in Atlanta in 1996.
Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie would write Half of a Yellow Sun, about the war, and give a talk heard around the world, We Should All Be Feminists.
Burna Boy would carry Nigerian pop across the world and win a Grammy for his album Twice as Tall.
In the early nineties, films shot fast and cheap on video gave birth to Nollywood, now one of the biggest film industries on Earth.
In 1999, the soldiers stepped back and civilian rule returned, the longest stretch of democracy in Nigeria's history.
Around the new century, a new sound took shape. By the 2010s, Afrobeats was filling dance floors far beyond Africa.
In 2014, the country was shaken when Boko Haram kidnapped two hundred and seventy-six schoolgirls from Chibok.
And in 2020, young Nigerians marched against a brutal police unit, until soldiers fired on protesters at the Lekki toll gate.
From Nok terracotta to Afrobeats, Nigeria's young and restless story is still unfolding.
